topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Which estate in land gives the owner the most complete form of ownership, with no time limit and no conditions on use or transfer?
choice_d: Fee simple subject to condition subsequent
explanation: Fee simple absolute is the highest form of ownership recognized in real property law: it is of unlimited duration, freely transferable, and inheritable, with no conditions attached to the grant.
source_note: Standard freehold estate doctrine (fee simple absolute), general U.S. property law/real estate licensing curriculum.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A grantor conveys land 'to the School District so long as it is used for school purposes.' If the land ceases to be used for a school, what happens to title?
choice_a: Nothing; the School District keeps fee simple absolute title
choice_b: It automatically reverts to the grantor or the grantor's heirs
choice_c: The grantor must file a lawsuit within one year to reclaim title
choice_d: Title passes automatically to the state as escheat
explanation: 'So long as' language creates a fee simple determinable. The grantor retains a possibility of reverter, and title reverts automatically the instant the stated condition is violated, with no legal action required.
source_note: Fee simple determinable / possibility of reverter doctrine, general U.S. real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A deed conveys property 'to the buyer, but if alcohol is ever sold on the premises, the grantor may retake the property.' This creates a:
choice_c: Fee simple subject to condition subsequent
explanation: Language giving the grantor the right (not the automatic effect) to retake the property upon breach of a stated condition creates a fee simple subject to condition subsequent, held together with a right of re-entry (power of termination) rather than an automatic reverter.
source_note: Fee simple subject to condition subsequent / right of re-entry doctrine, general U.S. real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A life estate is measured by the lifetime of someone other than the life tenant. This is known as an estate:
explanation: A life estate 'pur autre vie' (French for 'for the life of another') is measured by the life of a person other than the life tenant. When that measuring person dies, the estate ends, even if the life tenant is still living.
source_note: Life estate pur autre vie doctrine, general U.S. real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: When a life estate ends and the property is designated to go back to the original grantor (or the grantor's heirs), the grantor holds a future interest called a:
explanation: A reversion is the future interest retained by the grantor (or the grantor's estate) when the grantor conveys a lesser estate, such as a life estate, and the property is set to return to the grantor when that lesser estate ends.
source_note: Reversion vs. remainder distinction, general U.S. real property law (future interests).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A grantor conveys 'a life estate to my sister, then to my nephew in fee simple.' The nephew's future interest is called a:
explanation: When a life estate is granted and the property is set to pass to a third party (rather than back to the grantor) upon termination of the life estate, that third party holds a remainder interest.
source_note: Remainder interest doctrine, general U.S. real property law (future interests).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A life tenant in possession of property has a legal duty not to:
choice_a: Collect rent from tenants occupying the property
choice_b: Make ordinary repairs to maintain the property
choice_c: Commit waste that permanently damages the property's value for the remainderman
explanation: A life tenant is entitled to possession and to the income and ordinary use of the property, but owes a duty to the holders of the future interest (remainderman or reversioner) not to commit waste — that is, not to permanently damage or diminish the value of the property.
source_note: Life tenant's duty against waste, general U.S. real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Which of the following is a freehold estate rather than a leasehold (nonfreehold) estate?
explanation: Freehold estates (fee simple estates and life estates) involve ownership of indeterminate or lifetime duration. Estates for years, periodic tenancies, tenancies at will, and tenancies at sufferance are all leasehold (nonfreehold) estates involving a tenant's right of possession rather than ownership.
source_note: Freehold vs. leasehold estate classification, general U.S. real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A tenant signs a lease for a fixed term of exactly 12 months, beginning January 1 and ending December 31. This is an example of a(n):
explanation: An estate (tenancy) for years is a leasehold with a definite, agreed-upon beginning and ending date. Despite the name, it can be any fixed length of time, even less than a year, and it terminates automatically at the end of the stated term without notice.
source_note: Estate for years doctrine, general U.S. real property law (leasehold estates).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A month-to-month rental agreement that automatically renews for successive periods until either party gives proper notice to terminate is a:
explanation: A periodic tenancy continues for successive periods (such as month-to-month or year-to-year) and automatically renews unless one party gives the legally required notice of termination.
source_note: Periodic tenancy doctrine, general U.S. real property law (leasehold estates).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A tenant whose lease has expired continues to occupy the unit without the landlord's consent, and the landlord has not yet acted to evict. This tenant holds a:
explanation: A tenancy at sufferance (holdover tenancy) arises when a tenant who lawfully took possession remains in the property after the lease term ends without the landlord's consent. It is the lowest form of leasehold interest.
source_note: Tenancy at sufferance / holdover tenant doctrine, general U.S. real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A leasehold with no fixed duration that continues only as long as both the landlord and tenant agree, and which either party may terminate at any time, is a:
explanation: A tenancy at will has no set duration and exists only as long as both parties consent to it continuing; either party can terminate it, generally after providing whatever notice is required by state law.
source_note: Tenancy at will doctrine, general U.S. real property law (leasehold estates).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Which four unities must all be present at the time of creation for a valid joint tenancy?
explanation: A common-law joint tenancy requires the four unities of time (interests acquired at the same moment), title (acquired by the same instrument), interest (equal, identical shares), and possession (equal right to possess the whole property).
source_note: Four unities of joint tenancy, general U.S. property law (concurrent estates).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: The single most distinguishing feature of a joint tenancy, compared to a tenancy in common, is:
choice_a: The ability to hold unequal ownership shares
choice_c: The requirement that co-owners be married
choice_d: The right to mortgage the property without the other owner's consent
explanation: The right of survivorship means that when one joint tenant dies, that owner's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s) by operation of law, bypassing probate and any provision in the deceased owner's will.
source_note: Right of survivorship doctrine, general U.S. property law (joint tenancy).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Two owners hold title as tenants in common. Owner A owns a 75% interest and Owner B owns a 25% interest. This is permissible because tenancy in common does NOT require which unity?
choice_b: The right to sell one's own share
choice_d: The right to will one's share to heirs
explanation: Tenancy in common requires only unity of possession — each co-tenant has an equal right to possess the whole property — but co-tenants may hold unequal fractional interests, may have acquired title at different times, and by different instruments.
source_note: Tenancy in common unity requirements, general U.S. property law (concurrent estates).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A tenant in common dies. What happens to that owner's fractional interest in the property?
choice_a: It automatically passes to the surviving co-tenant(s)
choice_b: It escheats to the state immediately
choice_c: It is extinguished and the property reverts to the original grantor
choice_d: It passes to the deceased owner's heirs or beneficiaries under a will
explanation: Tenancy in common carries no right of survivorship. A deceased tenant in common's interest passes through probate to that owner's heirs or to the beneficiaries named in a will, just like any other asset.
source_note: Tenancy in common inheritance rules, general U.S. property law (concurrent estates).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: One of three joint tenants sells her interest in the property to an outside buyer. What is the resulting effect on title?
choice_a: The joint tenancy is severed as to that interest; the buyer holds as a tenant in common with the remaining two, who still hold a joint tenancy between themselves
choice_b: The sale is void because joint tenants cannot transfer their interest without unanimous consent
choice_c: The buyer automatically becomes a joint tenant with full survivorship rights with the other two owners
choice_d: The entire property must be partitioned and sold immediately
explanation: A joint tenant may convey their interest without the other owners' consent, but doing so breaks the unities of time and title as to that share. The new owner takes as a tenant in common, while the remaining original joint tenants continue to hold a joint tenancy among themselves (if more than one remains).
source_note: Severance of joint tenancy by conveyance, general U.S. property law (concurrent estates).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Tenancy by the entirety differs from joint tenancy chiefly in that it:
choice_a: Does not include a right of survivorship
choice_b: Is available only to married couples and requires a fifth unity of marriage
choice_c: Allows either owner to convey their interest unilaterally, severing the tenancy
choice_d: Requires the owners to hold unequal shares
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is a form of co-ownership available only to married couples (and, in some states, registered domestic partners). It requires the four unities of joint tenancy plus a fifth unity — marriage — and, unlike joint tenancy, neither spouse can unilaterally sever it or convey their interest without the other's consent.
source_note: Tenancy by the entirety doctrine, general U.S. property law (concurrent estates).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A co-owner who wants to end shared ownership of a property, but the other co-owners will not agree to sell, may generally ask a court to order a(n):
explanation: A partition action is a legal proceeding in which a court divides co-owned property among the owners (partition in kind) or orders it sold and the proceeds divided (partition by sale) when the co-owners cannot agree on how to end the co-ownership.
source_note: Partition action doctrine, general U.S. property law (concurrent estates remedies).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A deed conveys property to two unmarried buyers but is silent about the form of co-ownership intended. In most states, how will the buyers be presumed to hold title?
choice_a: As joint tenants with right of survivorship
explanation: Most states presume tenancy in common as the default form of co-ownership when a deed does not clearly express an intent to create a joint tenancy (with its right of survivorship) or another special form of ownership.
source_note: Default co-ownership presumption, general U.S. property law (concurrent estates).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Community property is a marital property system recognized in some U.S. states in which:
choice_a: Property acquired by either spouse during the marriage is generally owned equally by both spouses
choice_b: Only the spouse named on the deed has any ownership interest
choice_c: Property automatically passes to the surviving spouse regardless of a will
choice_d: Spouses cannot own property jointly under any circumstances
explanation: In community property states, property acquired by either spouse during the marriage (with limited exceptions such as gifts and inheritances) is generally considered owned equally by both spouses, regardless of whose name appears on the title.
source_note: Community property system overview, general U.S. property law survey content covered on national licensing exams.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A legal description that begins at a identifiable point of beginning and describes the parcel's boundaries using a sequence of directions (bearings) and distances back to that starting point is known as:
explanation: Metes and bounds describes a parcel's perimeter using courses (directions) and distances, starting and ending at a defined point of beginning, often referencing monuments (natural or artificial markers) along the way.
source_note: Metes and bounds legal description method, general U.S. real property law/surveying.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: In a metes and bounds description, natural or artificial landmarks referenced to fix boundary points (such as a large rock, a stream, or a fence post) are called:
explanation: Monuments are fixed natural or artificial objects used in a metes and bounds description to mark a corner or point along a boundary. They can supplement or, in the event of a conflicting measurement, take priority over stated courses and distances.
source_note: Monuments in metes and bounds descriptions, general U.S. real property law/surveying.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: The government (rectangular) survey system establishes its grid using which two controlling reference lines?
choice_a: A township line and a section line
choice_b: A metes line and a bounds line
choice_c: The equator and the international date line
choice_d: A principal meridian (north-south) and a base line (east-west)
explanation: The government survey system is built on a grid formed by a principal meridian, which runs north-south, and a base line, which runs east-west, intersecting at an initial point from which townships and ranges are measured.
source_note: Government (rectangular) survey system framework, general U.S. surveying/real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Under the government survey system, a standard township is a square parcel of land measuring:
explanation: A standard township is a 6-mile by 6-mile square, containing 36 square miles. Each township is further divided into 36 numbered sections, each approximately 1 square mile.
source_note: Township dimensions, government survey system, general U.S. surveying/real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Under the government survey system, one full section contains how many acres?
explanation: A section is approximately one square mile and contains 640 acres. A township is a 6-by-6-mile grid of 36 sections, numbered in a standardized boustrophedon (back-and-forth) pattern beginning in the northeast corner.
source_note: Section acreage, government survey system, general U.S. surveying/real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A parcel described as the 'NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4' of a section contains how many acres?
explanation: A section contains 640 acres. A quarter section is 160 acres (640 divided by 4), and a quarter of that quarter (a 'quarter-quarter') is 40 acres (160 divided by 4). The NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4 is a quarter-quarter section, so it contains 40 acres.
source_note: Government survey acreage calculation (quarter-quarter section), general U.S. surveying/real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A parcel described as the 'N 1/2 of the NE 1/4' of a section contains how many acres?
explanation: A quarter section contains 160 acres (640 acres divided by 4). Half of that quarter section (the N 1/2 of the NE 1/4) contains 80 acres (160 divided by 2).
source_note: Government survey acreage calculation (half of a quarter section), general U.S. surveying/real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: In the government survey system, rows of townships running north and south of the base line are called:
explanation: Rows of townships running east-west, numbered north or south of the base line, are called tiers (or township rows). Columns of townships running north-south, numbered east or west of the principal meridian, are called ranges.
source_note: Township tiers vs. ranges terminology, government survey system, general U.S. surveying.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A legal description that reads 'Lot 7, Block 3, Sunnyside Estates, as recorded in the plat records of the county' is an example of the:
explanation: The lot-and-block (recorded plat) method identifies a parcel by referring to its lot and block number on a subdivision plat map that has been surveyed and recorded with the county, most commonly used to describe parcels within platted subdivisions.
source_note: Lot-and-block (recorded plat) legal description method, general U.S. real property law/surveying.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Before land can be legally described using the lot-and-block system, what must first occur?
choice_a: The parcel must be assigned a township, range, and section number
choice_b: A metes and bounds survey must also be completed and attached
choice_c: A subdivision plat map must be surveyed, approved, and recorded with the county
choice_d: The property must be rezoned as agricultural
explanation: The lot-and-block system depends on a subdivision plat: a developer's surveyor divides a tract into numbered lots and blocks, and that plat map must be approved and recorded with the county before individual lots can be legally described and conveyed by lot and block number.
source_note: Plat recording as a prerequisite for lot-and-block descriptions, general U.S. real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Which legal description method is generally NOT considered adequate, by itself, for a deed because it can change over time and does not reliably identify precise boundaries?
explanation: A street address may help identify a property informally, but it is not considered a legally sufficient description for a deed because addresses can change, be duplicated, or fail to define precise boundary lines; deeds require metes and bounds, government survey, or lot-and-block descriptions.
source_note: Adequacy standards for legal descriptions in deeds, general U.S. real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A buyer purchases a house that includes a built-in dishwasher permanently wired and plumbed into the kitchen cabinetry. Absent a contrary agreement, this item is treated as:
choice_a: A fixture that conveys with the real property
choice_b: Personal property that the seller may remove before closing
choice_c: A trade fixture belonging to the seller
explanation: An item permanently attached to the real property in a manner that would cause damage or require significant effort to remove, and installed to enhance the use of the real property, is generally treated as a fixture that conveys with the property unless the sales contract states otherwise.
source_note: Fixture classification (method of attachment/adaptation), general U.S. real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Courts commonly weigh several factors to decide whether an item of personal property has become a fixture. Which of the following is NOT one of those factors?
choice_a: The method and permanence of attachment to the real property
choice_c: The intention of the party who installed the item
choice_d: Whether the item was adapted specifically for use with the real property
explanation: Courts typically weigh the method/permanence of attachment, the intention of the installing party, and adaptation of the item to the property's use (along with any express agreement between the parties). The item's original purchase price is not a legal test for fixture status.
source_note: Legal tests for fixture status (attachment, intention, adaptation), general U.S. real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A retail tenant installs display shelving and a walk-in cooler in a leased commercial space to run her business. These items are best classified as:
choice_a: Real property fixtures that automatically belong to the landlord
choice_c: Trade fixtures, which the tenant may remove before the lease ends
explanation: Trade fixtures are items a commercial tenant installs to conduct business. Even though they may be attached to the real property, the tenant retains the right to remove trade fixtures before the lease expires, provided the tenant repairs any damage caused by the removal.
source_note: Trade fixture exception for commercial tenants, general U.S. real property/landlord-tenant law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: If a seller and buyer disagree over whether a large mounted mirror bolted to a bathroom wall is a fixture, and the purchase contract is silent on the issue, whose intention generally controls in resolving the dispute?
choice_a: The intention of the real estate licensee handling the transaction
choice_b: Whichever party currently has physical possession of the property
choice_c: State statute always classifies wall-mounted items as personal property
choice_d: The intention of the person who originally installed the item, as evidenced by the manner and purpose of attachment
explanation: When a fixture dispute arises, courts look primarily to the objective intent of the party who attached the item — inferred from the method of attachment, adaptation to the property, and the relationship of the parties — rather than a later, self-serving claim of intent.
source_note: Intention test for fixture classification, general U.S. real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: The best practice to avoid a fixture dispute between a buyer and seller is to:
choice_a: Specifically list included and excluded items in the written purchase agreement
choice_b: Rely solely on the multiple listing service photos
choice_c: Assume all attached items automatically convey and all unattached items do not
choice_d: Wait until closing to discuss which items are included
explanation: Because fixture classification can be ambiguous, the safest approach is for the purchase agreement to expressly identify which items are included in the sale and which are excluded, removing any need to rely on the common-law tests.
source_note: Best-practice drafting to avoid fixture disputes, general real estate practice/licensing curriculum.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Riparian rights are water rights that generally belong to owners of land that:
choice_a: Is located anywhere within the same county as a river
choice_b: Borders a flowing waterway, such as a river or stream
choice_c: Has been granted a government water permit
explanation: Riparian rights are the rights of an owner whose land borders a flowing body of water, such as a river or stream, to make reasonable use of that water as it passes through or along the property.
source_note: Riparian rights doctrine, general U.S. real property law (water rights).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Littoral rights differ from riparian rights primarily in that littoral rights apply to land bordering:
choice_c: Large, relatively still bodies of water such as lakes, seas, or oceans
choice_d: Any body of water regardless of size or flow
explanation: Littoral rights belong to owners of land bordering large, substantially still bodies of water, such as lakes, seas, or oceans, whereas riparian rights apply to land along flowing waterways like rivers and streams.
source_note: Littoral rights vs. riparian rights distinction, general U.S. real property law (water rights).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A landowner whose property gradually gains additional land due to the slow deposit of soil by a flowing river is said to gain title to that new land through:
explanation: Accretion is the gradual, imperceptible addition of land to a property caused by the natural deposit of soil by water. The riparian or littoral owner generally gains title to this newly formed land.
source_note: Accretion doctrine, general U.S. real property law (water rights).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A sudden, violent event such as a flood or earthquake abruptly changes the course of a river, tearing away a significant portion of a landowner's property. This sudden loss of land is called:
explanation: Avulsion is the sudden, perceptible loss (or addition) of land caused by a dramatic natural event, such as a flood suddenly shifting a riverbed. Unlike accretion, ownership boundaries are generally NOT automatically adjusted to reflect the avulsive change.
source_note: Avulsion doctrine (contrasted with accretion), general U.S. real property law (water rights).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: The gradual recession of water from land (for example, a lake slowly shrinking and exposing more shoreline) that results in a landowner gaining additional land is known as:
explanation: Reliction (sometimes called dereliction) occurs when water gradually and permanently recedes, exposing previously submerged land, which then generally becomes the property of the adjoining riparian or littoral owner.
source_note: Reliction doctrine, general U.S. real property law (water rights).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: In many western U.S. states, water rights in rivers and streams have historically been allocated under a doctrine that grants rights based on who first put the water to beneficial use, regardless of whether their land touches the water. This is known as:
explanation: Prior appropriation ('first in time, first in right') is a water-rights doctrine common in many western states, under which the right to use water is based on historical priority of beneficial use rather than on ownership of land adjoining the water source.
source_note: Prior appropriation doctrine overview, general U.S. water law survey content (national real estate licensing curriculum).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Under the riparian rights doctrine, an owner's right to use adjoining water is generally limited by a standard of:
choice_a: Unlimited use with no consideration of downstream owners
choice_b: First-come, first-served priority regardless of land ownership
choice_c: Government permit only, with no common-law basis
choice_d: Reasonable use that does not unreasonably interfere with other riparian owners' use
explanation: The riparian doctrine generally entitles each riparian owner to make reasonable use of the water, balanced against the reasonable use rights of other owners along the same waterway, rather than granting any one owner unlimited or exclusive use.
source_note: Reasonable use standard under riparian doctrine, general U.S. real property law (water rights).

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes fee simple ownership from a leasehold estate?
choice_a: Fee simple is a form of ownership of the real property itself, while a leasehold is a tenant's right of possession for a limited period without owning the underlying land
choice_b: A leasehold always lasts longer than a fee simple estate
choice_c: Fee simple owners cannot lease their property to tenants
choice_d: There is no legal distinction; the terms are interchangeable
explanation: Fee simple is the greatest form of ownership interest in real property, of potentially unlimited duration. A leasehold estate is a tenant's non-ownership right to possess and use property for a defined or terminable period under a lease, while the landlord (lessor) retains the underlying fee ownership.
source_note: Fee simple vs. leasehold distinction, general U.S. real property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A property description combines a metes and bounds survey that references section and quarter-section lines from the government survey system. This illustrates that:
choice_a: Metes and bounds and government survey descriptions can never be used together
choice_b: The two legal description methods can be combined in a single description
choice_c: A lot-and-block reference is always required to make either method valid
choice_d: Government survey descriptions are illegal outside the original public land states
explanation: It is common, especially for irregularly shaped parcels within a section, for a metes and bounds description to begin its point of beginning at a corner established by the government (rectangular) survey system, combining elements of both methods in one legal description.
source_note: Combined use of metes and bounds with government survey reference points, general U.S. surveying practice.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: Which of the following best describes the historical geographic use of the metes and bounds description method in the United States?
choice_a: It is used exclusively in states west of the Mississippi River
choice_b: It was created specifically for use in subdivided residential developments
choice_c: It predominates in the original thirteen colonies and other eastern states, as well as Texas, which were settled before or outside the government rectangular survey system
choice_d: It applies only to commercial and industrial zoned parcels
explanation: Metes and bounds descriptions, inherited from English common law, remain common in the original thirteen colonies, other early eastern states, and Texas — areas settled before adoption of the government rectangular survey system or that never used it.
source_note: Geographic distribution of metes and bounds usage, general U.S. surveying history.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: A married couple takes title to their home as tenants by the entirety. If one spouse attempts to sell or mortgage the property without the other spouse's consent, that action is generally:
choice_a: Fully valid and binding on both spouses
choice_b: Valid only if recorded within 30 days
choice_c: Automatically converted into a tenancy in common
choice_d: Invalid, because neither spouse may unilaterally convey or encumber the whole property
explanation: Because tenancy by the entirety treats the married couple as a single legal owner, one spouse cannot unilaterally sell, mortgage, or otherwise encumber the property; both spouses must join in any conveyance or encumbrance.
source_note: Unity requirement / unilateral-conveyance restriction under tenancy by the entirety, general U.S. property law.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Interests & Legal Descriptions
question: An unmarried individual who owns real property outright, with no co-owners, and with no conditions limiting the duration of ownership, holds title as:
choice_a: A sole owner in fee simple absolute (severalty ownership)
choice_c: A tenant in common with the state
choice_d: A holder of a life estate
explanation: Ownership by a single person or entity, with no co-owners, is called ownership in severalty. When that sole owner holds the greatest possible interest with no time limit or conditions, the estate is fee simple absolute.
source_note: Ownership in severalty combined with fee simple absolute, general U.S. real property law.
